scenes.narration: This slide compares request selection inside an ALB target group. Start in the upper-left. Round robin distributes eligible requests sequentially across healthy targets and is a useful default when instances and request costs are similar. Move to the upper-right. Least outstanding requests favors targets that currently have fewer in-progress requests, making it useful when request duration or target processing capability varies. Now inspect the lower-left weighted random panel. Requests are distributed randomly with supported weighting behavior, and optional Automatic Target Weights can mitigate anomalous targets. The caveat in the panel matters: weighted random is not compatible with stickiness or slow start in the combinations shown. Finally, the lower-right illustrates session stickiness and target warmup. Cookies can keep a client associated with a target, but that affinity can introduce load imbalance. Slow start gradually increases traffic to a new healthy target using compatible target-selection settings. Do not confuse this per-target selection with weighted forwarding between different target groups during a deployment. The architecture decision is whether requests are comparable, how many are in flight, whether client affinity is essential, and how fresh targets become ready.

scenes.narration: The large title is an instruction for a safe shutdown, not just a load balancer setting. On the upper-left, the Application Load Balancer is routing to healthy instances. One target enters draining when it is deregistered, so new eligible work is directed away while in-flight requests have an opportunity to complete. Follow the dashed red arrow to the draining target and distinguish it from the blue arrows toward ready capacity. The upper-right stopwatch shows the deregistration delay. For ALB instance and IP target groups, the default is three hundred seconds and the configurable range is zero through thirty-six hundred seconds. That timer is a bounded opportunity, not a guarantee that every request finishes. In the lower-left panel, compare container shutdown grace, application worker termination and long-running connection behavior. Killing a process early can still interrupt an active request regardless of the load balancer's timer. Finally, the lower-right panel shows the correct rollout order: start replacements, verify readiness, shift incoming work, drain old targets, then terminate. Include health alarms and rollback checks. A graceful release coordinates the load balancer and the application rather than relying on a single default timeout.

scenes.narration: This is a deployment architecture using two application versions behind an Application Load Balancer. Begin with the central gold control and the two fleets labeled V one and V two. The ALB listener's forward action can assign relative weights to separate target groups, gradually increasing traffic toward a new version while retaining old capacity. The first lower panel gives a ninety-to-ten example. These weights express a statistical intended share of new requests, not an exact percentage in every small sample. The next panel introduces target-group stickiness. A client may remain associated with a selected group, so existing sessions need not immediately follow revised weights. Now read the yellow warning. If a weighted target group is empty or entirely unhealthy, the ALB does not automatically redirect all of that group's assigned traffic to another healthy group. You need health monitoring and an active deployment decision. Finally, the rightmost panel shows rollback. Monitor errors, latency and business transactions, and restore safe weights if behavior deteriorates. But redirecting traffic does not undo database migrations or restore incompatible state. Weighted forwarding is a useful release control only when application health and data compatibility are already engineered.
